:::{#lem-euclidean-lattice-qcd .callout-note icon="false"}
## Euclidean Lattice QCD Path Integral

Starting from the Minkowski QCD Lagrangian with gauge group $G=SU(3)$,
one may perform a Wick rotation $t=-i\tau$ and obtain the Euclidean
path integral
$$
\begin{align}
Z
=
\int \mathcal D A\,\mathcal D\bar\psi\,\mathcal D\psi\,
\exp\left[-S_E[A,\bar\psi,\psi]\right].
\end{align}
$$

On a Euclidean hypercubic lattice with spacing $a$, the continuum gauge
field is replaced by link variables
$$
\begin{align}
U_{x,\mu}
=
\mathcal P\exp\left(
i g\int_x^{x+a\hat\mu} A_\mu(s)\,ds
\right)
\in SU(3),
\end{align}
$$
which transform under a local gauge transformation $\Omega_x\in SU(3)$ as
$$
\begin{align}
U_{x,\mu}
\mapsto
\Omega_x U_{x,\mu}\Omega_{x+\hat\mu}^{\dagger}.
\end{align}
$$

The elementary plaquette is
$$
\begin{align}
U_{x,\mu\nu}
=
U_{x,\mu}
U_{x+\hat\mu,\nu}
U_{x+\hat\nu,\mu}^{\dagger}
U_{x,\nu}^{\dagger}.
\end{align}
$$

The Wilson gauge action is
$$
\begin{align}
S_g[U]
=
\frac{\beta}{N_c}
\sum_{x}\sum_{\mu<\nu}
\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}
\left(
\mathbf 1-U_{x,\mu\nu}
\right),
\qquad
\beta=\frac{2N_c}{g^2}.
\end{align}
$$

For small lattice spacing,
$$
\begin{align}
U_{x,\mu\nu}
=
\exp\left(
i g a^2 F_{\mu\nu}(x)+O(a^3)
\right),
\end{align}
$$
and hence
$$
\begin{align}
S_g[U]
=
\frac{1}{2}
\int d^4x\,
\operatorname{Tr}\left[
F_{\mu\nu}(x)F_{\mu\nu}(x)
\right]
+
O(a^2),
\end{align}
$$
up to normalization conventions for the generators.

Adding lattice fermions gives a fermion action
$$
\begin{align}
S_f[U,\bar\psi,\psi]
=
\sum_{x,y}\bar\psi_x M_{x,y}[U;m,\mu]\psi_y,
\end{align}
$$
where $M[U;m,\mu]$ is a lattice Dirac operator, for example Wilson,
staggered, domain-wall, or overlap Dirac operator. Integrating out the
Grassmann fields gives
$$
\begin{align}
Z
=
\int \mathcal D U\,
e^{-S_g[U]}\det M[U;m,\mu].
\end{align}
$$

At zero baryon chemical potential, the fermion determinant can be made
real and nonnegative in standard flavor settings. Then
$$
\begin{align}
\pi[U]
=
\frac{1}{Z}
e^{-S_g[U]}\det M[U;m,0]
\end{align}
$$
defines a probability measure over gauge-field configurations, enabling
importance-sampling Monte Carlo methods such as Hybrid Monte Carlo.

At nonzero real baryon chemical potential, however,
$$
\begin{align}
\det M[U;m,\mu]\in\mathbb C,
\end{align}
$$
in general. Therefore the weight
$$
\begin{align}
e^{-S_g[U]}\det M[U;m,\mu]
\end{align}
$$
is not a positive probability distribution. This is the finite-density
sign problem of lattice QCD.
:::
